summary: Explain Newton’s third law of motion with respect to stress and deformation.

sections.title: Hooke’s Law: Stress and Strain Revisited
objectives: Explain Newton’s third law of motion with respect to stress and deformation.
Describe the restoration of force and displacement.
Calculate the energy in Hooke’s Law of deformation, and the stored energy in a spring.

misconceptions.claim: A pendulum swings faster when it is given a bigger push.
misconceptions.correction: The period of a pendulum does not depend on the push. It depends on the length and on gravity.

summary: An oscillation is a back and forth motion of an object between two points of deformation.
An oscillation may create a wave, which is a disturbance that propagates from where it was created.

The simplest type of oscillations and waves are related to systems that can be described by Hooke’s law: F=−kx, where F is the restoring force, x is the displacement from equilibrium or deformation, and k is the force constant of the system.

sections.title: Period and Frequency in Oscillations
objectives: Observe the vibrations of a guitar string.
Determine the frequency of oscillations.

misconceptions.claim: The frequency of an oscillation is the time taken for one complete cycle.
misconceptions.correction: That is the period. The frequency is the number of cycles in one second, and the two are reciprocals, so a wave of $50\,\text{Hz}$ has a period of $0.02\,\text{s}$.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-3, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the period as the frequency.

misconceptions.claim: A wave of frequency $50\,\text{Hz}$ has a period of $2\,\text{s}$.
misconceptions.correction: The period is the reciprocal of the frequency, $T = 1/f = 1/50 = 0.02\,\text{s}$. Multiplying the two instead of dividing gives the wrong figure.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-4, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the multiplied reading as an option.

summary: Periodic motion is a repetitious oscillation.
The time for one oscillation is the period T.
The number of oscillations per unit time is the frequency f.

sections.title: Simple Harmonic Motion: A Special Periodic Motion
objectives: Describe a simple harmonic oscillator.
Explain the link between simple harmonic motion and waves.

misconceptions.claim: In simple harmonic motion the acceleration is constant.
misconceptions.correction: The acceleration is a = −ω²x, so it changes with position. It is maximum at the extremes and zero at equilibrium.
misconceptions.signal: Only constant-force motion has constant acceleration.

misconceptions.claim: A simple harmonic oscillator moves at constant speed.
misconceptions.correction: Its speed varies. It is zero at the extremes and maximum as it passes through equilibrium.
misconceptions.signal: The velocity changes direction every half cycle.

summary: Simple harmonic motion is oscillatory motion for a system that can be described only by Hooke’s law. Such a system is also called a simple harmonic oscillator.
Maximum displacement is the amplitude X. The period T and frequency f of a simple harmonic oscillator are given by T=2πmk and f=12πkm, where m is the mass of the system.
Displacement in simple harmonic motion as a function of time is given by x ( t ) = X cos 2π t T .

sections.title: The Simple Pendulum
objectives: Measure acceleration due to gravity.
Use the simple pendulum to measure g and explain why its period is independent of mass.

misconceptions.claim: A wave carries energy along with it.
misconceptions.correction: A wave carries energy but not matter. The medium stays where it is, and the energy travels through it.

summary: A mass m suspended by a wire of length L is a simple pendulum and undergoes simple harmonic motion for amplitudes less than about 15º. The period of a simple pendulum is T=2πLg,where L is the length of the string and g is the acceleration due to gravity.
Explain Newton’s third law of motion with respect to stress and deformation.
Describe the restoration of force and displacement.

authored_exercises.stem: Does the period of a simple pendulum depend on the mass of its bob?
authored_exercises.answer: No. For small swings the period depends on the length and on g, not on the mass.
solution: The restoring force is proportional to the weight.
The mass cancels in the equation of motion.

sections.title: Energy and the Simple Harmonic Oscillator
objectives: Determine the maximum speed of an oscillating system.
Apply conservation of energy to find the speed of an oscillator at a given displacement.

misconceptions.claim: The total energy of an undamped oscillator changes as it swings.
misconceptions.correction: The total energy is constant. Kinetic and potential energy interchange, but their sum stays the same.
misconceptions.signal: Energy is conserved when damping is negligible.

misconceptions.claim: At maximum displacement the kinetic energy is maximum.
misconceptions.correction: At maximum displacement the oscillator is momentarily at rest, so the kinetic energy is zero and all the energy is potential.
misconceptions.signal: Speed is zero at the turning points.

summary: Energy in the simple harmonic oscillator is shared between elastic potential energy and kinetic energy, with the total being constant: 1 2 mv 2 + 1 2 kx 2 = constant.
Maximum velocity depends on three factors: it is directly proportional to amplitude, it is greater for stiffer systems, and it is smaller for objects that have larger masses: vmax=Xkm

authored_exercises.stem: At which point in simple harmonic motion is the kinetic energy maximum?
solution: The speed is greatest at equilibrium.
Kinetic energy is ½mv², so it is maximum there.
At the extremes the speed is zero and all the energy is potential.

sections.title: Uniform Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Motion
objectives: Compare simple harmonic motion with uniform circular motion.
Explain how simple harmonic motion is the projection of uniform circular motion.

misconceptions.claim: Simple harmonic motion is the same as uniform circular motion.
misconceptions.correction: SHM is the projection of uniform circular motion onto a diameter. The projection’s speed varies, while the circular motion’s speed is constant.
misconceptions.signal: The circular motion is a mathematical model for the projection.

summary: A projection of uniform circular motion undergoes simple harmonic oscillation.
Explain Newton’s third law of motion with respect to stress and deformation.
Describe the restoration of force and displacement.

authored_exercises.stem: A point moves uniformly on a circle of radius 0.2 m at angular speed 3 rad/s. Its projection on a diameter executes simple harmonic motion. Find the amplitude and maximum speed of the projection.
solution: The amplitude of the projection equals the circle’s radius, 0.2 m.

sections.title: Damped Harmonic Motion
objectives: Compare and discuss underdamped and overdamped oscillating systems.
Explain critically damped system.

misconceptions.correction: Damping gradually removes energy and reduces the amplitude. Critical damping returns the system to equilibrium quickly without overshooting; overdamping returns it more slowly.
misconceptions.signal: The type of damping changes the return, not just the speed.

misconceptions.claim: An overdamped system oscillates more slowly than a critically damped one.
misconceptions.correction: An overdamped system does not oscillate at all. It returns to equilibrium without crossing it, often more slowly than the critical case.
misconceptions.signal: Overdamping means too much damping for oscillation.

summary: Damped harmonic oscillators have non-conservative forces that dissipate their energy.
Critical damping returns the system to equilibrium as fast as possible without overshooting.
An underdamped system will oscillate through the equilibrium position.

sections.title: Forced Oscillations and Resonance
objectives: Observe resonance of a paddle ball on a string.
Observe amplitude of a damped harmonic oscillator.

misconceptions.claim: At resonance the amplitude grows forever.
misconceptions.correction: The amplitude peaks near the natural frequency, but damping limits it. A sustained driving force keeps supplying energy; without it, damping eventually removes the motion.
misconceptions.signal: Resonance is a large response, not unlimited energy.

summary: A system’s natural frequency is the frequency at which the system will oscillate if not affected by driving or damping forces.
A periodic force driving a harmonic oscillator at its natural frequency produces resonance. The system is said to resonate.
The less damping a system has, the higher the amplitude of the forced oscillations near resonance. The more damping a system has, the broader response it has to varying driving frequencies.

sections.title: Waves
objectives: State the characteristics of a wave.
Calculate the velocity of wave propagation.

misconceptions.claim: A wave carries matter along with its energy.
misconceptions.correction: A wave carries energy and momentum, but the medium oscillates about fixed positions and does not travel with the wave.
misconceptions.signal: Watch a floating cork: it bobs but does not ride the wave to shore.

misconceptions.claim: The speed of a wave depends on its frequency.
misconceptions.correction: In a given medium the wave speed is set by the medium. Changing the frequency changes the wavelength, not the speed.
misconceptions.signal: v = fλ keeps the product fixed.

summary: A wave is a disturbance that moves from the point of creation with a wave velocity vw.
A wave has a wavelength λ, which is the distance between adjacent identical parts of the wave.
Wave velocity and wavelength are related to the wave’s frequency and period by v w = λ T or v w = fλ .

authored_exercises.stem: State the relationship between wave speed, frequency and wavelength.
solution: The wave travels one wavelength in one period.
Frequency is the reciprocal of the period.

sections.title: Superposition and Interference
objectives: Explain standing waves.
Describe the mathematical representation of overtones and beat frequency.

misconceptions.claim: Two superposed waves always make a larger wave.
misconceptions.correction: Superposition adds displacements algebraically. In-phase waves add constructively; exactly out-of-phase waves cancel.

misconceptions.claim: A standing wave travels along the medium.
misconceptions.correction: A standing wave has fixed nodes and antinodes. Energy is trapped between the nodes rather than transported along the medium.
misconceptions.signal: The pattern stays in place while the medium oscillates.

summary: Superposition is the combination of two waves at the same location.
Constructive interference occurs when two identical waves are superimposed in phase.
Destructive interference occurs when two identical waves are superimposed exactly out of phase.

sections.title: Energy in Waves: Intensity
objectives: Calculate the intensity and the power of rays and waves.
Calculate wave intensity from power and area, and explain the inverse-square falloff.

misconceptions.claim: Intensity and power are the same quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Intensity is power per unit area. A source of the same power gives a smaller intensity when spread over a larger area.

misconceptions.claim: The intensity of a spherical wave is the same at every distance.
misconceptions.correction: It falls as 1/r² because the same power spreads over a sphere of area 4πr².
misconceptions.signal: Doubling the distance quarters the intensity.

summary: Intensity is defined to be the power per unit area:

sec-4:exr-85.stem: A 90.0-kg skydiver hanging from a parachute bounces up and down with a period of 1.50 s. What is the new period of oscillation when a second skydiver, whose mass is 60.0 kg, hangs from the legs of the first?

sec-4:exr-31.stem: A babysitter pushes a child on a swing. At the instant the swing is momentarily at rest at one extreme of its motion, where is the corresponding point on a displacement-time graph of the motion?
sec-4:exr-31.answer: At a crest or a trough: the displacement is at its maximum amplitude.
solution: The extreme of the swing is the point of maximum deformation, which corresponds to the amplitude of the motion.
On a displacement-time graph that point is either at the very top or the very bottom of the curve, depending on which extreme is chosen.
sec-4:exr-31.solution_provenance: OpenStax CNXML solution element (in file); the unnamed point X in the source is described explicitly

sec-5:exr-50.answer: (a) 2.99541 s (b) $T∝g^{-1/2}$, so a 1% change in $g$ changes $T$ by about 0.5%; at least five significant figures are needed to see the shift.
solution: (b) Since $T=2π\sqrt{L/g}$ , $T∝g^{-1/2}$. For small changes, $ΔT/T≈-\frac{1}{2}Δg/g$. A 1% change in $g$ therefore changes the period by about 0.5%, not 0.01%, so several decimal places are needed to resolve it.
sec-5:exr-50.solution_provenance: OpenStax CNXML solution element (in file); the source's $(0.01)^2=0.01%$ sentence is corrected to the square-root dependence

sec-5:exr-62.answer: 2.45 h per revolution; the clock runs slow by a factor of 2.45.
solution: A minute hand that takes 1.00 h per revolution on Earth takes 2.45 h per revolution on the Moon, so the clock runs slow by a factor of 2.45.
sec-5:exr-62.solution_provenance: OpenStax CNXML solution element (in file); the source answer gave only the factor, not the time the question asks for

sec-2:exr-35.stem: Which of the following represents the distance (how much ground the particle covers) moved by a particle in simple harmonic motion in one time period? Here $A$ represents the amplitude of the oscillation.
solution: In one period the particle moves from one extreme to the other and back again, a total distance of $A+A+A+A=4A$.
